knitr::opts_chunk$set(

A vignette to help understand how to use PsyR to enact Post-Hoc Analysis of Variance via Confidence Intervals in a within-subjects design [@bird2004]. This technique adopts a multivariate approach, assuming a lack of spherecity in the data (as is necessarily expected in within-subjects designs).

## The Packages

To use Psy to calculate confidence intervals over contrast effects, we will utilise a workflow with functions from [afex](https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/afex/versions/1.4-1) to implement ANOVA models, and [emmeans](https://rvlenth.github.io/emmeans/) to obtain estimated marginal means and the required contrast estimates. So let's load those packages, and any others that are helpful for our workflow.


```{r setup, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE}
library(afex)
library(emmeans)
library(PsyR)
library(tidyverse)
```

## The Data

The kevin_within dataframe contains data from a single-factor within-subjects experiment assessing the impact of a treatment on patient wellbeing. N = 5 participants were recruited. They were measured pre-treatment, post-treatment, and at a 6 month follow-up. Thus, the dependent variable (wellbeing) has p = 3 levels.

Lets load the data, then call the `head()` function to print the first 5 rows.

```{r loaddata}
data(kevin_within)
head(kevin_within, 5)
```

To learn more about the kevin_within dataframe call the help function using `?df` to open its documentation.


```{r, whatfatigue, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, eval = FALSE}
?kevin_within
```

When working with this dataframe, we need the data to be in long-form. So, call `pivot_longer()`, assigning names to a new "Session" column and values to a new "Score" column. We also will call `fct_relevel()`, assigning the "Session" column as a factor and reordering the levels of the independent variable according to chronological order.

```{r longform}
kevin_within <- kevin_within %>%
  pivot_longer(c("Pre", "Post", "FU"),
    names_to = "Session",
    values_to = "Score"
  )

kevin_within <- kevin_within %>%
  mutate(
    Session = fct_relevel(
      Session, 
      "Pre", 
      "Post", 
      "FU"
    )
  )
head(kevin_within, 5) %>%
  knitr::kable(format = "html", table.attr = "style='width:50%;'")
```

Next, let's visualise our data. Doing so allows us to understand the overall layout of the data, which can be used to inform which contrasts should be analysed.

```{r boxplotit, fig.width = 7.1, fig.height = 4}
kevin_within %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = Session, y = Score, fill = Session)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  theme_classic(base_size = 14)
```

## The Analysis

Lets prepare to run some statistical tests!

Here we will create the building blocks for first an ANOVA output, and later our CIs. This workflow can be justified as follows.

The folloing code builds towards this approach.

The following code builds towards an eventual SCI approach. Let's create a new object *emms*, calling the `emmeans()` function and specifying that we want to take in *mod* (the object we just made) and output according to "Group" (which, as a reminder, is a column of the factor datatype which indicates what level of the IV each score belongs to). Running this code will give us the estimated marginal means for each level of the independent variable.

First, lets specify that we want a multivariate analysis, using the `afex_options()` function. Next, lets create a new object *mod* by calling the `aov_ez()` function which takes in the "Subject" column to identify subjects, the "Score" column as the dependent variable, the kevin_within dataframe, and the "Group" column set as between-subjects. Next, lets create a new object *emms*, calling the `emmeans()` function and specifying that we want to take in *mod* (the object we just made) and output based upon "Session". Running this code will give us the estimated marginal means for the dependent variable (wellbeing) at each level of the independent variable (time of measurement).

```{r model}
# set emmeans option to multivariate
afex_options(emmeans_model = "multivariate")

# perform the statistical model
mod <- aov_ez(
  "Subject",
  "Score",
  kevin_within,
  within = "Session"
)

emms <- emmeans(mod, "Session")
knitr::kable(emms, digits = 3)
```

Time to define our contrasts!

With only p = 3 levels of the independent variable, it makes sense to define simple contrasts examining the difference between each level. Of note, the post-hoc nature of our analysis prevents inflation of the Type I error rate, meaning that in designs with more levels of the IV it is valid to define as many contrasts as are deemed of interest. With all that being said, the following three contrasts are chosen for analysis

- "Post - Pre" ➞ The difference between scores taken pre- and post-intervention.
- "FU - Post" ➞ The difference between scores taken post-intervention and at a 6 month follow-up.

- "FU - Pre" ➞ The difference between scores taken prior to intervention and at a 6 month follow-up.

Having defined our contrasts, let's store them within a contrasts table. Create the *cnt_res* object, then call the `contrast()` function from the emmeans package, setting *emms* in the "object" argument and *contrasts* in the "method" argument (which will take in our newly defined contrasts). The output of this code, as shown below, contains the results of hypothesis tests of each contrast.

```{r phoc}
contrasts <- list(
  "Post-Pre" = c(-1, 1, 0),
  "FU-Post"  = c(0, -1, 1),
  "FU-Pre"   = c(-1, 0, 1)
)

cnt_res <- contrast(emms, contrasts)
knitr::kable(cnt_res, digits = 3)
```

### The (Initial) Interpretation

Fill in

Such analysis establishes that significant effects exist in our chosen contrasts, but does not allow for specific insight into the magnitude of said effects. An approach utilising CIs can remedy this. To achieve this with PsyR, let's create an object *contrasts_w_cis* using the `psyci()` function, specifying the following:


Finally, lets compute our post-hoc 95% CIs for our within-subjects design. To do so, lets call `psyci()` from the PsyR package, specifying the following:

- The model is specified as the previously made *mod* object, where the model must be made using the afex package - afex_aov.

- The contrast_tables argument is set as the previously made *cnt_res*.

- The method is set as "ph", creating confidence intervals (estimate +- SE x cc) using a post-hoc method [@bird2004a].

- The family list is set as "w", specifying that the contrast table is within-subjects.

- The within_factors argument is set according to our desired group names, as in the "Session" column.

```{r, scis}
psyci(
  model = mod, 
  contrast_tables = cnt_res, 
  method = "ph", 
  family_list = list("w"),
  within_factors = list("Session")
) %>%
knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

## The Interpretation

There is insufficient evidence to suggests a significant difference exists in any of our contrasts of interest (p \> 0.05). However, our SCIs can give us some insight into the directionality of our data.

- Compared to pre-intervention, scores at post-intervention may have improved by up to 6.192 units, or may have regressed by 0.192 units.

- Compared to post-intervention, participants at follow up may have improved by up to 16.636 units, or may have regressed by 10.636 units.

- Compared to pre-intervention, participants at follow up may have improved by up to 17.836 units, or may have regressed by 5.836 units.
